sections.text: A String works as an error for small programs, but an enum describes exactly what went wrong and lets callers react to each case.
Each arm handles one kind of error. The Locked arm also pulls out the minutes stored inside the variant.

To print an error with {}, its type needs to implement Display. Display is a trait. A trait is a named set of abilities or methods that a type promises to have, and many types can share one. Display is the one that says "this type can be shown to a person with {}". You give a type a trait by writing impl Trait for Type and filling in the methods the trait asks for. Traits get a whole unit later (Unit 7), so for now just follow the pattern.

Display asks for one method, fmt. Copy its first line exactly as shown. Inside, write! works like println!, but instead of printing to the screen it writes the text into f, the formatter Rust hands you. write! gives back a fmt::Result saying whether that worked, and fmt returns it, so there's no semicolon after it.

Error types usually also implement the standard std::error::Error trait. It has no methods you must write, but it requires Debug and Display. So for a LoginError that also has #[derive(Debug)], impl std::error::Error for LoginError {} is enough; without Debug it won't compile. It lets your error work with Box<dyn Error> and with other libraries.

From is another standard trait. impl From<ParseIntError> for ConfigError tells Rust how to build a ConfigError out of a ParseIntError (the type in angle brackets is what you convert from). The ? operator uses it automatically: when parse fails, ? turns the ParseIntError into a ConfigError before returning it.
ParseIntError implements Display too, which is why {e} prints a readable message.
This lesson pulls together enums, match, impl and Result, and gives you a first taste of traits. If it feels like a lot, that's normal. Come back to it after Unit 7.
In real projects, the thiserror crate generates Display and From for error enums, and anyhow gives applications a convenient catch-all error type.

exercise.prompt: main already prints the error with {e}, which needs ShopError to implement Display. Add a Display impl for ShopError, following the LoginError example, with the message "out of stock". It should print: Error: out of stock

tests.label: OutOfStock displays as out of stock
The program prints Error: out of stock
Display on a reference
Display is not the Debug text

hints: Look at how LoginError gets a readable message: an impl block with one method inside. ShopError needs the same, with only one variant to handle.
Write impl fmt::Display for ShopError and copy the fmt line exactly as in the lesson. Inside, match self with one arm for ShopError::OutOfStock that calls write!(f, "...").
Use write!(f, "out of stock") with no semicolon after it. main already prints with {e}, and that is what uses your message.
